newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Canada says U.S. appears to be blackmailing U.N..
newsitem.headline: Canada says U.S. appears to be blackmailing U.N..

text.p: In an apparent reference to the United States, Canada said some countries appeared to be blackmailing the United Nations by withholding funds as a means of enacting changes through fiscal starvation.

In his address to the U.N. General Assembly, Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said that tight budgets were no excuse to withhold dues. His own country had taken some of the most severe fiscal cuts in the industrial world and still paid up.
"Perhaps some members are withholding dues as a form of blackmail, hoping to pressure the United Nations into reforms through fiscal starvation," he said.
"This is both wrong-headed and short-sighted. An organisation in crisis will not have the energy required to tackle genuine reform," he said.

The United States owes $1.6 billion dollars in arrears for peacekeeping and regular dues, more than half of the world body's total debt of $2.8 billion. The U.S. Congress has tied U.N. reforms to making payments toward the debt and has unilaterally put a ceiling on how much Washington will pay.
President Bill Clinton earlier on Tuesday alluded to toward the United Nations in the Republican-dominated Congress and blamed opponents for difficulties in paying the bill.
"We are paying our dues and we are committed to paying off our accrued obligations soon," Clinton told the assembly.

Axworthy's comments on the U.S. debt were among the toughest in this year's General Assembly session, equalled only by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, who on Monday bluntly told the assembly that refusal to pay dues amounted to intimidation.

The minister said the United Nations was not doing enough work to investigate human rights abuses. Therefore Canada would immediatel create a list of qualified Canadian human rights experts available for rapid deployment in larger U.N. operations.

"Sustainable human security means providing basic needs in both economic and political ways," he said. "Respect for human rights and democratic principles is fundamental to the prevention of conflict and to post-conflict reconstruction."
"Nowhere has this lesson been learned more clearly or more grimly than in Rwanda and in Bosnia."
